source_title: Man shares strict chore list his dad made him follow from age 8
source_excerpt: A two-page document from childhood has brought back memories for some adults and started a debate among parents about how much responsibility children should have at home.The document was shared by an Instagram Threads user, @fatcarl_sp, who posted a picture of the chore list his father had prepared for him when he was just eight years old. What makes the post interesting is not just the number of tasks, but how carefully his father had structured his day."My dad sent me my chore list from when I was a kid.. this started at 8 years oldâ¦ my pop was the coolest man on earth but he had hella structure & rules in the house," he wrote.The post quickly caught attention, with more than a million views, as people looked at the old-school routine and compared it with the way children are raised today.A two-page document that covered his entire dayUnlike a casual reminder to help around the house, the father's list was a detailed, typed-out document spread across two pages. It was divided into different sections, covering the child's morning routine, a checklist for leaving the house on time, and responsibilities for evenings and weekends.Some of the instructions were straightforward but specific. He was expected to make his bed as soon as he woke up, take out the trash and do his own laundry.The list was organised enough to resemble a daily schedule rather than a collection of occasional chores. It also suggested that the father expected his son to follow certain routines without waiting for someone else to remind him.For the man sharing it years later, however, the memory came with affection rather than resentment. He described his father as the coolest man on earth, even while acknowledging the strict structure and rules at home.That contrast is perhaps what made the post particularly interesting to people online: a childhood remembered fondly, but one that also came with a clearly defined set of responsibilities. View on ThreadsWhy some parents loved the listThe reactions to the post showed how differently people view childhood chores.One commenter said they wanted to know what consequences the father had for not completing a task. The person explained that offering children an allowance for doing chores had not worked in their own household and was considering introducing additional consequences.Another user recalled growing up with a mother who did everything for her. While that may have seemed convenient as a child, she said it left her struggling to manage everyday responsibilities as an adult."As a child whoâs mom did everything for her, this is amazing. I canât tell you how much I struggled as an adult at first trying to figure out everything I had to do, and also not be overwhelmed by it bc my mom did EVERYTHING for us growing up," the commenter wrote.She added that children need to understand that household work is simply part of life.Another parent praised the approach, recalling having a chore list for their own children. They explained that responsibilities included keeping the kitchen clean and completing homework, although the family also had social commitments and the tasks were not necessarily an everyday requirement.For some, the post also brought a little regret. One commenter said they wished their parents had introduced similar structure while they were growing up, adding that at 19, they were still struggling with cleanliness while living with their fiancÃ©.A familiar parenting debate: Structure or too many rules?The discussion goes beyond whether an eight-year-old should make a bed or take out the garbage. It touches on a question many parents face: how early should children be expected to contribute to running a household?Some see a chore list as a practical way of teaching children that a home does not maintain itself and that everyone has a role to play. Others may feel that a detailed schedule risks making childhood overly structured.Research has also explored the possible developmental benefits of age-appropriate household responsibilities. A 2019 study published in the Journal of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics found associations between children performing chores in kindergarten and better self-perceived competence, social relationships and academic outcomes in third grade. The findings do not establish that chores directly cause these improvements, but they offer another perspective on why everyday responsibilities can matter.Perhaps the most interesting thing about the viral post is that the man did not share the list as a complaint about his childhood. He remembered his father warmly, even as he recalled the rules that came with growing up in his house.And that is what has made people look at the document and reflect on their own childhoods: some remember being given too much to do, others wish they had been taught more, and many are now wondering where to draw the line with their own children.You use AI every day.
